subject: music
title: Transcription and Modulation by Ear
welcome_lead: From listening to notation — the A-Level aural skill.
meta_desc: A-Level Music: melodic dictation, modulation recognition.

concepts.def: Writing down music heard, by ear.
Notated music written from oral source — usually one line.
Change of key — heard via cadence in new key.
Move between major and its relative minor (C to Am).
Move to the key a 5th above (C to G).
Hearing the moment when a chord pivots between two keys.

walkthroughs.body_html: First hearing: shape and metre. Second: cadences and tonal plan. Third: details (rhythm, contour). Fourth: check. Most exam dictations are 4-8 bars at moderate tempo.
Most tonal modulations move to: dominant (C→G), relative minor (C→Am), relative major (Am→C), subdominant (C→F), or by chromatic mediant (C→E).
Listen for a perfect cadence in the new key — V7-I in the new tonic confirms arrival. Strong A-Level answers identify the modulation moment by bar.

mcqs.q: What does modulation mean in music?
options: Changing from one key to another within a piece.
Changing tempo or dynamics.
It is always C major.
Adjusting volume electronically.

mcqs.q: How do you identify a major key from its key signature?
options: ii to V.
The last sharp is the leading note (semitone below tonic); the second-to-last flat is the tonic.
The number of sharps or flats equals the tonic note number.
It is always C major.

mcqs.q: Which chords form a plagal cadence?
options: IV to I (the 'amen' cadence).
V to I.
ii to V.
It is always C major.
